newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan strait links more political than economic.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan strait links more political than economic.

text.p: The likely end of a 48-year-old ban on shipping across the Taiwan strait -- possibly in April -- is politically significant in the longstanding and still-bitter rivalry between Taiwan and China.

But economically, the effect is limited because Taipei, acutely suspicious of Beijing's intentions, will allow only transshipments of cargoes between China and third countries, not direct cross-strait exchanges, analysts said on Thursday.

Nationalist-ruled Taiwan has banned all direct contacts with the communist mainland since a civil war split them in 1949, but has come under intense pressure from Taiwan's thousands of investors in the mainland to ease the restrictions.

Taipei is expected as early as Friday to allow the first of five mainland shippers, Fujian Foreign Trade Centre Shipping Co, to ply a direct route between southern Taiwan's Kaohsiung port and Xiamen in China's Fujian province, Taiwan sources said.
Beijing is reviewing similar applications by a dozen Taiwan shippers and is expected to issue the first approvals almost simultaneously, shipping sources and analysts said.
"The beginning of cross-strait shipping has great political meaning," China-watching economist Chung Chin of the Chunghua Institution for Economic Research told Reuters.

Chung said cross-strait links would effectively end Taiwan's ban on direct shipping, despite Taipei's insistence that the breakthrough is something less because it involves only "offshore transshipments" that remain outside Taiwan customs.
Taiwan insists that mainland cargoes be allowed only to be processed at a newly established "offshore transshipment centre" for onward shipment to other destinations.
It also requires that the ships be registered in Hong Kong or foreign countries and will not allow ships flying China's red five-star flag into its ports.

Beijing, while calling the route a domestic matter between Chinese provinces, has settled on a similar formula so that ships flying the flag of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China do not sail into mainland ports.

Experts said Taipei's refusal to allow direct cargo exchanges limited the economic viability of the direct route, since all of the huge and growing trade flows between Taiwan and the mainland still would have to cross via Hong Kong.
Spokesmen M.S. Tsay of Taiwan giant Yangming Marine Transport Corp said the breakthrough nevertheless would bring some cost savings to shippers.

"Take Yangming for example. Containers transshipped through Kaohsiung instead of Hong Kong should cost less by US$100 to US$150," Tsay said, explaining that Yangming operates its own highly efficient loading facilities at Kaohsiung.
Another Yangming official estimated that the company could save up to US$3 million a year after the link was established.

While Beijing sees direct links as a success in its quest to bring Taiwan under communist sovereignty, Taipei is far more cautious, fearing that over-dependence on its rival's economy investments would increase Taiwan's political vulnerability.
Taiwan is already vulnerable in trade. The island's 1996 exports to Hong Kong were US$26.805 billion -- most of it destined for China -- while imports were just US$1.705 billion.
Trade with China represents about 10 percent of Taiwan's total foreign trade, according to official Taiwan figures.
